questions.question: Why would a team create a partitioned Pulsar topic instead of adding only more consumers to a non-partitioned topic?
options: A partitioned topic creates internal topic lanes that can be served by multiple brokers, increasing producer-side throughput.
Partitions make every message globally ordered.
Partitions move subscription cursors out of BookKeeper.
Partitions automatically choose the correct subscription type.
questions.explanation: A non-partitioned topic has one broker owner. A partitioned topic is implemented as multiple internal topics that can be distributed across brokers. Subscription semantics remain a separate decision.

questions.question: Independent image-resize jobs can run on any worker and do not require ordering. Which subscription is the clearest starting point?
options: Exclusive
Failover
Shared
A unique subscription name for every worker
questions.explanation: Shared allows multiple consumers on one subscription and distributes messages among them. It intentionally does not promise ordering, which matches independent work.

questions.question: Customer events must remain ordered per customer while different customers run in parallel. Which design matches that invariant?
options: Shared with no message keys
Key_Shared with a stable customer key and key-based batching or batching disabled
Exclusive with one subscription per process
Failover with a random key on every event
questions.explanation: Key_Shared assigns one key to one consumer at a time. The producer must preserve key boundaries in batching so the broker can maintain that assignment.

questions.question: A partitioned topic has six partitions and a Failover subscription with ten connected consumers. How many consumers can be active at once for that subscription?
options: One total
At most six, one active consumer per partition
All ten on every partition
Exactly sixteen
questions.explanation: Failover selects one active consumer for each partition. With six partitions, at most six consumers are active and the rest provide standby capacity.

questions.question: A namespace uses E=3, W=3, A=2. What does A=2 mean for a new ledger entry?
options: The broker reports success after two durable BookKeeper writes acknowledge the entry.
Only two brokers may serve the namespace.
The entry is written to exactly two topic partitions.
Two consumers must acknowledge before the producer succeeds.
questions.explanation: The ack quorum is the number of successful BookKeeper writes required before the broker acknowledges the producer. It is unrelated to consumer acknowledgments.

questions.question: The broker owning a persistent topic crashes after the producer received a publish acknowledgment. Why is the message not stored uniquely on that broker?
options: The producer keeps the only copy forever.
Persistent entries and subscription cursors are stored in BookKeeper, while another broker can recover topic ownership.
The metadata store contains the complete message payload.
Tiered object storage is always the synchronous write path.
questions.explanation: Pulsar separates serving from storage. Brokers own client connections and dispatch; BookKeeper stores persistent ledger entries and cursor state.

questions.question: What is the difference between backlog and retention in Pulsar?
options: They are two names for the same policy.
Backlog is unacknowledged data required by a subscription; retention can deliberately keep acknowledged data for later access.
Retention applies only to non-persistent topics.
Backlog is stored only in broker memory.
questions.explanation: Unacknowledged messages form subscription backlog. A retention policy keeps acknowledged data beyond that point; tiered storage can reduce the hot-storage cost of long retention.
